master.title: How France-Russia Relations Could Affect the Security of the Baltic Sea Region
master.content:
President of France, Emmanuel Macron, whose country is currently holding the presidency of the Council of the European Union, does not want the EU to be relegated to the background behind NATO and the US. He wishes to demonstrate his ability to oppose Russia while also maintaining dialogue with Moscow.

This will be difficult but given that France and Russia may encounter each other in operational areas in Africa, the Middle East and Asia Minor, it is feasible. Even his most recent visit to Moscow, although not achieving a breakthrough, showed that both sides are ready to talk. Macron confirmed commitments from both Vladimir Putin and Volodymyr Zelenskyy to respect the Minsk agreements.

Macron’s Russia Policy to Date

The French President has never been anti-Russian. He has repeatedly called for dialogue with the Russian Federation and even put his trust in the creation of new structures. His predecessors, including Nicolas Sarkozy, who pointed out that the lack of rapprochement with Russia was pushing it into the arms of China, were of a similar opinion.

Despite direct rivalries in Africa and the Middle East in recent years, both Putin and Macron have been able to discuss problems and challenges effectively. Moreover, tensions on other continents have not adversely affected French and Russian interests in Europe. The two powers maintain ongoing relations at the level of the highest representatives through a 2+2 format of dialogue (ministers of defence and foreign affairs), as well as by being open to mutual investment.

France and Russia are testing the limits of their influence on the security of Central and Eastern Europe. The Normandy format has proved ineffective. Therefore, arrangements are being made during bilateral talks between Moscow and Paris. Macron has assumed the role of the main intermediary between the Kremlin and other states. In the past, Angela Merkel played a significant role, whereas Putin is now communicating mainly with the French President. Consequently, any issue concerning the security of the continent when threatened by Russian troops will be negotiated by the Élysée Palace. Macron used to know how to talk to Putin. However, the meeting at the beginning of February showed that he has lost some of this ability.

On the one hand, the fact that Russia reckons with the EU’s leading country in the field of defence when it comes to its actions, and that the French President is able to stand up to the Kremlin’s demands, is clear and obvious. On the other hand, France has proved more than once that its national interests are a priority. Macron cannot constantly balance between Moscow, Washington and Brussels. As far as domestic politics is concerned, he manages to dodge the issues of radicalisation and migration. On the international arena, however, the time to take sides is approaching.

A European Army

Macron acknowledged that only Europe can assert real sovereignty and defend its own interests and values. However, the ability to do so must be constantly developed. With this statement, the president clearly shows that it is France’s vision to build a defence capability for the continent. Moreover, it is no secret that Macron seeks to create a “true European army” that would not depend on external, hegemonic powers treating Europe as a centre of rivalry. The new army would provide protection against China, Russia and even the influence of the US.

The creation of the EU army is one of Macron’s prime objectives, which he intends to implement if elected for a second term. This initiative can be supported by the Baltic states, by Estonia, as well as the Takuba Task Force partners who maintain good relations with France, such as the Czech Republic, Denmark, Greece, Romania and Italy. In addition, there are other countries also maintaining relations with Paris, namely Austria and Poland. Under these circumstances, France, with the largest army in the EU and raising its GDP on defence to 3%, could develop the necessary structures on its own and consider the Eurocorps its initiative. Such an army would be deployed to protect the borders of the European Union starting with the EU’s eastern border.

The Baltic States and French Politics

The military involvement of France in Estonia is a key factor in maintaining security in the Baltic states. The presence of the multinational NATO brigades constitutes part of the deterrence strategy, yet it is the French operability within LYNX (including international military exercises) that demonstrates its willingness to be active in the region and readiness to compete militarily with Russia. The military support of France, which openly admits that Russia cannot be as bold as to dare any aggression against NATO and EU member states, makes it possible for the Baltics to concentrate on other challenges. The French Republic will not protect Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia from disinformation, the influx of migrants, cyberattacks and energy crises. However, they can expect bilateral cooperation, including mutual support in Africa and as part of multinational military exercises.

The Baltic states should look at the attempt to re-shape the security architecture and France-Russia relations as an opportunity to build their sovereignty and independence. Favouritism in NATO and the politics of Macron seeking support in EU countries will enable the formation of their own structures and goals on the international arena. The Eastern Flank is a political, military, economic and social foundation. The security of the Baltic states will be essential for France in its struggle with Russia. Their stability will make it possible to concentrate on further strategic points, such as Ukraine, the Baltic Sea and the Balkans. France has already let Mali and Burkina Faso go. In addition, Russia wants to shape Europe by deciding who may or may not join individual alliances, and Macron knows he should stop that.

Election in France and its Aftermath

Should Macron or Valérie Pécresse win the 2022 French presidential election, the situation is not expected to deteriorate. Russia is in a difficult position, among other things, because of its declining economy, social dissatisfaction and substantial concentration on too many battlefields.

In the case of a victory for Marine Le Pen or Éric Zemmour (despite such scenarios being unlikely), the French political line will shift significantly towards Moscow. Nevertheless, this will not fundamentally change the security situation of the Baltic states, which will maintain their relations with Paris and will be further secured by the NATO alliance.

Views expressed in ICDS publications are those of the author(s).
